items.prompt: How does wind carve smooth, rounded shapes into exposed desert rock over long stretches of time?

options.label: It hurls sand grains against the rock, and each tiny impact wears away a speck of the surface
options.feedback: Grain after grain of sand, carried and flung by the wind, strikes the rock and chips away an almost invisible amount of material with every impact, and countless impacts add up to a rounded, worn shape.

options.label: It heats and cools the rock unevenly until it cracks apart
options.feedback: Uneven heating and cooling does stress rock, but that is a separate process driven by sunlight, not by anything the wind itself is doing as it passes.

options.label: It dissolves the surface of the rock chemically as it blows past
options.feedback: Air alone has no chemical action on solid rock. Wind wears rock down mechanically, by striking it with carried particles, not by dissolving it.

options.label: It presses down on the rock with enough force to crush its surface
options.feedback: Moving air exerts far too little direct pressure to crush stone. The shaping comes from what the wind is carrying and flinging against the rock, not from the air's own weight.

items.ok_line: Countless sand grains flung against the rock wear it down, one tiny impact at a time.
items.ko_title: Think about what the wind is carrying
items.ko_line: Wind alone is nearly powerless against solid rock. Ask what it picks up along the way and hurls against the surface instead.
items.exp_text: As wind sweeps across loose desert ground it lifts and carries countless grains of sand, and where that moving sand strikes an exposed rock face, each grain chips away a minute fragment of the surface on impact. Repeated over years by a wind that generally blows from the same direction, those countless tiny impacts smooth and round the rock into the sculpted shapes found across many deserts.

items.prompt: Why does wind-blown sand rarely rise more than about a metre above the desert floor, even in a strong sandstorm, while dust from the same storm can be carried thousands of metres high?

options.label: Sandstorms only occur where the ground is perfectly flat
options.feedback: Sandstorms happen across dunes, gravel plains and uneven desert terrain alike, so flatness of the ground is not what limits how high the sand itself travels.

options.label: Sand grains are heavy enough that wind can only bounce and skip them close to the ground, while dust particles are light enough to be lifted and carried far above it
options.feedback: Wind moves sand mainly by knocking one grain into the next in low, bouncing hops close to the surface, because the grains are too heavy to be lifted much higher, whereas much lighter dust particles can be picked up bodily and carried far up into the moving air.

options.label: Sand is magnetically drawn back toward the ground
options.feedback: Ordinary desert sand has no meaningful magnetic property pulling it downward. What keeps it low is simply its weight relative to the force of the wind.

options.label: Dust particles repel each other and push themselves upward
options.feedback: Dust particles do not repel one another in any way that would lift them. They rise because the wind itself is capable of carrying something so light, not because of any force between the particles.

items.ok_line: Heavy sand bounces low; light dust is carried high.
items.ko_title: Compare the weight of the two
items.ko_line: Sand grains and dust particles differ enormously in weight, and that difference decides how far off the ground the wind can lift each one.
items.exp_title: Two sizes, two very different rides
items.exp_text: A grain of sand is far too heavy for ordinary wind to lift straight up, so instead the wind knocks it forward in short, low bounces, each landing grain often striking and dislodging another in a hopping chain close to the surface. A speck of dust, by contrast, is light enough that once it is stirred into the air the wind can hold it aloft and carry it upward on rising currents, which is how desert dust ends up drifting thousands of metres high and travelling across entire oceans.

items.prompt: Why do sand dunes so often form ripples across their surface, spaced at fairly regular intervals?

options.label: Rain periodically washes grooves into the sand at fixed distances
options.feedback: Deserts where these ripples form are typically far too dry for rain to be a regular shaper of the surface, and rainfall would erode a random pattern rather than a regular one anyway.

options.label: Buried rocks beneath the surface create bumps at even spacing
options.feedback: Ripples form just as readily on deep, uniform sand with nothing buried beneath it, so hidden rocks cannot be the general explanation.

options.label: Bouncing sand grains tend to travel a similar hop distance before striking the surface again, and each landing spot builds up into a tiny ridge that then shapes the next hop
options.feedback: Grains skipping across the surface in the wind tend to cover a fairly consistent distance in each hop, and wherever landing grains pile up slightly, that small ridge disturbs the next grains enough to reinforce a regular, evenly spaced pattern of ripples.

options.label: Insects burrowing under the sand push up evenly spaced mounds
options.feedback: Ripple patterns appear across vast stretches of lifeless desert sand with no burrowing insects present at all, so animal activity cannot be the general cause.

items.ok_line: A consistent hop distance for bouncing grains builds itself into a regular ripple pattern.
items.ko_title: Think about the hopping sand grains
items.ko_line: Sand does not simply slide across a dune — it moves in short hops, and those hops tend to cover a similar distance each time.
items.exp_title: A rhythm built from countless similar hops
items.exp_text: Wind moves sand across a dune mainly by bouncing grains forward in short hops of a fairly consistent length, and wherever slightly more grains happen to land than move on, a tiny ridge begins to build. That small ridge then disturbs the next arriving grains just enough to encourage them to land and pile up at a similar distance beyond it, and repeated many times over this self-reinforcing rhythm produces the evenly spaced ripples seen rolling across a dune's surface.

items.prompt: Why does a sand dune slowly creep forward across the desert over months and years, rather than staying in one fixed place?

options.label: The whole dune is picked up and set down again as a single block
options.feedback: A dune never moves as one solid block. It advances through the much slower, grain-by-grain motion of countless individual particles being shifted across its surface.

options.label: Underground water currents drag the base of the dune along
options.feedback: Most dune-forming deserts have no meaningful underground water movement at this scale, and even where groundwater exists, it has no grip on loose surface sand strong enough to drag a dune.

options.label: The dune's own weight causes it to slide downhill under gravity alone
options.feedback: Most dunes rest on relatively flat or gently sloping desert floor, with nowhere near enough incline for gravity alone to slide the whole mass forward without the wind's help.

options.label: Grains are continually blown up the gentler windward slope and then tumble down the steeper far side, so the whole shape gradually shifts downwind
options.feedback: Wind steadily carries grains up the dune's long, gentle upwind face, and once they tip over the crest they slide down the much steeper slope on the far side, and repeated endlessly this shifts the entire dune's shape a little further downwind each time.

items.ok_line: Grains climb the gentle slope and tumble down the steep one, shifting the whole dune downwind.
items.ko_title: Think about the dune's two different slopes
items.ko_line: A dune has one long, gentle side facing the wind and one short, steep side facing away from it. Ask what happens to grains carried up the gentle side once they reach the top.
items.exp_title: Climbing one face, tumbling down the other
items.exp_text: Wind steadily pushes sand grains up the dune's long, gently sloped windward face, and once enough grains gather near the crest they tip over and slide down the far steeper slope on the sheltered side, a slope held at close to the steepest angle loose sand can maintain before collapsing. As this cycle repeats endlessly, grain by grain, sand is removed from the windward face and added to the sheltered one, and the entire dune's shape is carried a little further downwind with each repetition.

items.prompt: Why does a fence or line of shrubs planted across a sandy, windy area often cause a small dune to build up right beside it?

options.label: The obstacle slows the wind passing through and around it, and slower wind can no longer carry as much sand, so grains drop out and pile up near the barrier
options.feedback: As wind is forced through or around a fence or line of shrubs, its speed drops noticeably in the sheltered zone just beyond, and slower-moving air has less carrying power, so sand it was holding aloft settles out and begins to accumulate right there.

options.label: The fence releases a chemical that attracts sand
options.feedback: An ordinary fence or line of shrubs releases nothing that could chemically attract sand grains drifting past on the wind.

options.label: The fence is magnetically charged by friction with the wind
options.feedback: Wind rubbing against a fence generates no meaningful magnetic charge, and even if it did, ordinary sand has no magnetic property that would respond to it.

options.label: Sand naturally settles fastest wherever a barrier casts a shadow
options.feedback: Shade blocks sunlight, not wind, and it is the wind's carrying power, not the presence or absence of shadow, that determines where sand drops out of the air.

items.ok_line: Slowed wind loses its carrying power, and the sand it was holding settles out right there.
items.ko_title: Think about what a barrier does to wind speed
items.ko_line: An obstacle in the path of the wind changes how fast the air is moving nearby, and that speed is what decides how much sand the wind can still carry.
items.exp_text: A fence or line of shrubs disturbs the smooth flow of wind passing through or over it, and in the sheltered zone just downwind the air moves noticeably slower than the open wind approaching it. Because a slower wind can hold far less sand aloft than a faster one, grains that were being carried steadily along suddenly find themselves in air too weak to keep carrying them, and they drop out and accumulate into a small dune hugging the barrier.

items.prompt: Why can thick layers of a fine, fertile soil called loess, found across parts of several continents, be traced back to wind rather than to rivers or glaciers?

options.label: Loess is found only on mountaintops, far above where rivers or glaciers could ever reach
options.feedback: Loess deposits actually occur mainly across plains and lowlands rather than on mountaintops, so elevation alone is not the clue pointing to a windborne origin.

options.label: Loess deposits are made almost entirely of extremely fine, similarly sized particles with no pebbles or coarse material mixed in, the kind of sorting only a long, steady, airborne journey produces
options.feedback: Because wind can only keep the very lightest, finest particles aloft over great distances, dropping the coarser material long before it travels far, the particles that finally settle out far from their source are remarkably fine and uniform in size — a signature that neither a river nor a melting glacier, both of which deposit a much wider mix of particle sizes together, tends to leave behind.

options.label: Loess always contains seashells, proving it settled from ocean water
options.feedback: Loess deposits are typically found far inland and do not generally contain seashells, and their defining feature is the fineness and uniformity of their particles, not any marine content.

options.label: Loess is always the exact same colour as the bedrock directly underneath it
options.feedback: Loess frequently sits on top of bedrock of an entirely different colour and composition, because the particles were carried in from elsewhere by wind rather than forming from the rock directly beneath.

items.ok_line: Uniformly fine particles, sorted by a long airborne journey, are wind's signature.
items.ko_title: Think about what a long ride on the wind does to particle size
items.ko_line: Wind can only carry the very lightest particles over great distances, and that limitation leaves a distinctive mark on what finally settles out far from its source.
items.exp_title: A fingerprint left by sorting in the air
items.exp_text: As dust is lifted and carried by wind over long distances, only the finest, lightest particles stay aloft the whole journey, while anything heavier drops out much closer to its source, so what finally settles far downwind is left strikingly uniform in size. Rivers and melting glaciers, by contrast, typically dump a jumbled mix of fine and coarse material together in the same place, so a deposit made up of consistently fine, well-sorted particles points to a long, steady journey carried by wind rather than to water or ice.

items.prompt: Why do trees growing on an exposed, constantly windy coastline or ridge often end up permanently bent and leaning, all pointing the same direction?

options.label: The trees were planted at an angle deliberately
options.feedback: Wind-bent trees appear even in places with no history of planting at all, including remote, unplanted coastlines, so deliberate angling by a planter cannot be the general explanation.

options.label: Lightning strikes on exposed ridges bend trees permanently
options.feedback: Lightning strikes an individual tree only rarely and would more likely split or kill it outright rather than gradually bending its whole shape in one consistent direction over many years.

options.label: Constant wind pressure kills the buds and shoots on the side of the tree facing into it, so growth continues mainly on the sheltered side and the tree leans away from the wind over years
options.feedback: New growth on the side of the tree exposed to the steady, drying wind is repeatedly damaged and stunted, while growth on the sheltered side continues largely unimpeded, and over years that lopsided growth bends the whole tree's shape away from the prevailing wind.

options.label: Roots on one side of the tree simply grow deeper than the other
options.feedback: Root depth differences do not by themselves bend a tree's visible trunk and branches in one consistent direction — what shapes the visible lean is what happens to growth above ground, facing the wind.

items.ok_line: Growth stunted on the windward side and unimpeded on the sheltered side bends the tree away from the wind.
items.ko_title: Think about which side of the tree struggles to grow
items.ko_line: The wind does not simply push the tree over — it acts on new growth differently depending on which side faces into it, year after year.
items.exp_title: A shape built one growing season at a time
items.exp_text: On an exposed, constantly windy site, the buds and young shoots on the side of a tree facing directly into the wind are repeatedly battered and dried out, so they grow slowly or fail altogether, while shoots on the sheltered side grow comparatively freely. Season after season, that imbalance in where new growth can succeed steadily shifts the tree's overall shape away from the wind, leaving a permanently lopsided, leaning form that points in the same direction as its sheltered neighbours.

items.prompt: Why does wind-driven erosion strip topsoil from a plowed farm field far faster than it does from a neighbouring field left covered in grass?

options.label: Plowed soil is chemically different from soil left under grass
options.feedback: The chemical composition of the soil itself does not meaningfully change simply because it has been plowed. What changes is how loose and exposed the particles are, and whether roots and cover are protecting them.

options.label: Grass fields always receive more rainfall than plowed fields nearby
options.feedback: Neighbouring fields receive essentially the same rainfall, since rain does not select between plowed and grass-covered ground. Rainfall is not what accounts for the difference in wind erosion.

options.label: Wind blows in a different direction over plowed soil than over grass
options.feedback: The wind passing over two neighbouring fields blows from the same general direction regardless of what is planted in either one. Direction of the wind is not what changes between them.

options.label: Bare, loosened soil has nothing anchoring its particles or blocking the wind at ground level, while grass roots bind the soil together and its leaves slow the wind right at the surface
options.feedback: A network of grass roots holds soil particles together against the wind's pull, and the grass blades themselves break up and slow the wind exactly where it would otherwise be strongest, right at ground level, while bare, loosened soil offers no such resistance on either count.

items.ok_line: Roots bind the soil and leaves slow the wind at ground level; bare soil has neither.
items.ko_title: Think about roots and ground-level wind together
items.ko_line: Two things protect soil from wind at once — something holding the particles together, and something slowing the air that would otherwise carry them off.
items.exp_title: Two protections, both missing from bare soil
items.exp_text: Grass holds soil in two ways at once: its roots weave through the ground and physically bind particles to their neighbours, resisting the wind's pull, while its leaves and stems form a low, dense cover that slows the wind dramatically in the thin layer of air right at the surface, where erosion does its work. Plowed, bare soil has neither protection, so wind blowing across it meets loose, unanchored particles in fast-moving air with nothing to hold them down, and it strips the topsoil away far more readily than it can from ground still covered in grass.

items.prompt: Why do windblown sand dunes typically form only where there is a steady supply of loose, dry sand and a fairly steady wind direction, rather than in every sandy place?

options.label: A dune needs a continuous stock of movable grains and a wind that keeps piling them the same general way; without either one, the sand simply spreads thin or gets scattered in every direction instead of building upward
options.feedback: Building a dune's characteristic mounded shape requires enough loose sand arriving steadily to keep adding height, and a wind that keeps depositing it in roughly the same place and orientation rather than scattering it evenly in every direction, and losing either the supply of sand or the consistency of wind direction leaves the sand spread thin instead of piled into a dune.

options.label: Dunes can only form directly beside an ocean
options.feedback: Dunes form far inland across many of the world's deserts, hundreds of kilometres from any coastline, so proximity to the ocean is not a requirement.

options.label: Dunes require soil that has been recently plowed by farmers
options.feedback: The vast majority of the world's dune fields lie in uninhabited desert, entirely untouched by farming of any kind, so plowed soil cannot be a general requirement.

options.label: Dunes form only where the ground beneath the sand is perfectly level
options.feedback: Dunes form across desert floors with considerable variation in underlying shape, from gently sloped basins to areas among low outcrops of rock, so a perfectly level base is not required.

items.ok_line: A dune needs a steady supply of sand and a wind that keeps depositing it consistently.
items.ko_title: Think about supply and consistency together
items.ko_line: Building a mound rather than a thin, scattered layer of sand needs two things at once: enough loose grains arriving, and a wind that keeps piling them up the same way.
items.exp_title: Two ingredients, both needed to build height
items.exp_text: A dune only grows taller if loose sand keeps arriving faster than the wind carries it away, giving the pile a continuous supply to build from, and if the wind blows from a fairly consistent direction so that arriving grains are stacked in roughly the same place instead of being spread out evenly in every direction. Where either the sand supply runs thin or the wind direction shifts constantly, sand tends to stay scattered across the surface rather than gathering into the tall, organised mounds that mark a true dune field.

items.prompt: Why do isolated pillars and arches of rock, left standing alone in some windswept deserts, often have a noticeably narrower base than top?

options.label: Rain always falls harder on the upper part of a rock formation
options.feedback: In the arid deserts where these formations typically stand, rainfall is scarce overall and does not consistently fall harder on the upper portion of a rock pillar than on its base.

options.label: Sand-carrying wind is concentrated closer to the ground, where the bouncing, heavier grains travel, so that band wears away the rock fastest while the wind higher up, carrying only fine, sparse dust, wears the upper section far more slowly
options.feedback: Since heavier sand grains are mostly bounced along close to the surface while the air higher up carries only much lighter, sparser dust, the band of rock nearer the ground meets a far more abrasive, sand-laden wind than the rock above it, and over time that band erodes away faster, leaving the base narrower than the top.

options.label: The rock at the base is always a softer type of stone than the rock at the top
options.feedback: Many of these formations are carved from a single continuous layer of the same rock type from base to top, so a difference in rock hardness cannot be the general explanation for the narrowed base.

options.label: Underground roots slowly eat away at the base from below
options.feedback: These pillars typically stand in barren desert with no significant plant roots reaching their base, so root activity cannot account for the narrowing seen across so many such formations.

items.ok_line: Heavier sand stays low and wears the base fastest; only fine dust reaches higher up.
items.ko_title: Think about where the sand itself travels
items.ko_line: Sand grains and dust do not ride at the same height in the wind. Ask which band of the rock meets the more abrasive material more often.
items.exp_title: A narrow band of wind doing most of the wearing
items.exp_text: Sand grains, too heavy to be lifted far, travel mainly in a low band close to the ground, bouncing and striking anything in their path, while the air higher up carries mostly fine, much less abrasive dust. A rock pillar standing in that wind therefore has its lower section sandblasted far more intensely than its upper section over the same stretch of time, and as the base wears away faster than the top, the whole formation is gradually left narrower where the sand-laden wind does its heaviest work.
